newsitem.title: UK: EU work ruling seen having little impact on UK.
newsitem.headline: EU work ruling seen having little impact on UK.

text.p: The European Court ruling that Britain should comply with the 48-hour maximum working week directive will have little if any impact on the UK labour market or the competitiveness of the economy, analysts said on Tuesday.

"My feeling is that, like a lot of social contract issues, the 48-hour working week will be a guideline not a law. Those who want to ignore it will do so and the impact will be minimal," said Simon Briscoe, UK economist at Nikko Securities.

The EU's working time directive, upheld by the European Court of Justice on Tuesday, states that the average maxiumum work week should be 48 hours, but workers may put in more time on a voluntary basis.
The directive exempts a wide range of workers, including those from transport, sea workers and doctors in training.
The government vociferously attacked the ruling. Trade and Industry Secretary Ian Lang said the directive would cost British industry up to 2.0 billion stg.
And Prime Minister John Major said the government would halt progress of any new agreements at the Intergovernmental Conference next year if the UK was not protected from the regulations.
Immediately after the ruling, business leaders queued up to say it would damage British business and competitiveness.

"The working time directive will restrict businessmen's ability to run their companies competitively and successfully," said Ruth Lea, head of the policy unit at the Institute of Directors, an employers' lobby.
"Moreover the increase in record keeping will be especially burdensome for small and medium sized companies, today's job creators, and only service to stifle employment growth."
But independent economists said the impact of the ruling would be miniscule, providing the directive is not the first of several steps to reduce the working week further.

"This regulation alone will have only a tiny impact on the labour market," said Michael Dicks, UK economist at Lehman Brothers. "Only if this is a first step to reduce the work week further, say to 40 hours, would it start to be detrimental."
But Nikko's Briscoe said that if the regulations became compulsory they would start to harm Britain's flexible employment market.
"If the ruling has teeth it will be damaging to the flexibility of the labour market. You cannot increase workers' rights and increase the flexibility of the labour market at the same time."
Employers' groups called for the government to make full use of the exemptions written in to the directive.
UK workers notched up an average 39.5 hours per week in the spring of 1996, according to the latest Labour Force survey.
Recent figures from European Commission suggest a higher level of 43.4 per week, making Britons the longest working employees in the EU.
German workers averaged 39.9 and French employees 39.7. Belgium and Italy brought up the rear with 38.2 hours.

But economists said given the widespread labour market reforms of the 1980s which reduced power of trade unions, along with the growing trend for part-time and short-term contracts, employees are less confident about keeping their jobs, so are less likely to fight for their new-found rights.

"In today's labour market it's not likely that people will be articulating their rights as much as they have in the past, so even if they don't want to work over 48 hours they'll keep quiet about it," said one analyst.
And Dicks said the apparently changing relationship between trade unions and employers means a compromise may be sought.
"We've seen TUC officials this week at the CBI conference sounding like they are looking for common ground with employers rather than looking for a fight with them."
The opposition Labour Party said on Tuesday the government was playing party politics with the issue.

"I think it is artificial indignation from a Government that is going to implement the directive, that actually negotiated the dilution of the directive in the first place," said opposition employment spokesman David Blunkett.
"It is trying to use what are very modest measures to protect the rights of the individual in a way that they hope will create an anti-European feeling."
